_comment: Canned evidence for the offline self-check. The HTML is real and gets parsed for real; the network parts and the ARIA snapshot are fixed so the score is deterministic. aria_snapshot strings mirror what Chromium actually produces, including the fact that a placeholder supplies an accessible name of last resort and a bare input beside a styled div does not.
_lens_comment: expected_lens_bands are recorded from a run, not predicted, so they are a regression tripwire. div_soup is the case that justifies the split: it reads as a C for an assistant and a D for an agent trying to operate it, and the old single number averaged that difference away.

null_state._comment: A page neither an assistant nor an agent can use. Controls are present and broken rather than absent, so every operability signal scores rather than dropping out: div-onclick widgets instead of buttons, inputs whose labels are styled divs, unnamed interactive nodes. A WAF serves the plain UA a 403 while the browser UA gets 200, which is exactly what A2 exists to catch and is what takes the last partial credit off the board. Both lenses band F and the headline is 0. This is the product's core promise as a fixture: if AI cannot see you, we score you 0, not 8.

no_controls._comment: A legitimate static article: nothing wrong with it, simply nothing for an agent to operate. D1, D2 and D3 have nothing to measure, so they drop out of the operability denominator, leaving A2 alone: 8 of 33 points, under the evidence floor. The lens must report no score at all rather than 100 for having no faults. This is the case the old full-marks-for-absence behaviour got wrong on every content page in the world.
